summary: This informational document describes use cases and call flows for the SIP History-Info header field, which records the Request-URIs as a SIP request is retargeted. It gives call flow diagrams and messaging details.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone call gets passed from desk to desk, this shows a diary that records each stop, with worked examples.

questions: what is the sip history-info header
when to use history-info in sip
subtitle: Documenting how SIP records the path a call takes when retargeted.

tldr.problem: In SIP, calls are often retargeted (forwarded to different addresses) as they travel through the network. An application needs to know the path the call took to understand why it arrived where it did.
tldr.mechanism: The History-Info header field, defined in RFC 7044, records the Request-URI (the address each stage tried to reach) as a SIP request is retargeted. Each entry includes the URI, an index number, and optional parameters that indicate why the retargeting happened and which entry triggered the current attempt.
tldr.outcome: Applications and voicemail systems can now examine the history to understand the call path, avoid duplicating attempts, determine which alias was used, and provide better service to users.

today: RFC 7131 is an informational document that provides guidance and examples for using the History-Info header field from RFC 7044. History-Info is optional in SIP, and adoption varies by vendor and use case. The call flow examples remain relevant for anyone implementing SIP applications that need to understand call routing.

sections.title: How Calls Get Rerouted
sections.content:
Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is the protocol for setting up phone calls, video calls, and other real-time sessions over the Internet. A call request often passes through one or more proxy servers, which may retarget the call to a different address based on local rules, redirects, or location information.

For example, Alice calls Bob at sip:bob@example.com. The example.com proxy looks up Bob and finds he has registered three locations: his desk phone, his office phone, and his home phone. The proxy may try each in sequence. Each time the proxy retargets the call to a new address, a new branch of the request is created. From Alice's perspective, she sees a sequence of responses as each attempt is made. The History-Info header field lets Alice (or an application) understand which addresses were tried and in what order.
sections.plainLanguage: A call travels through the phone system and gets sent to different places. History-Info is a record that tags along and says 'I tried this desk, then that office, now trying home.'

sections.title: The History-Info Header Field
sections.content:
Each entry in the History-Info header records a URI (the address that was tried), an index (a number that shows the order and hierarchy), and optional parameters. The main parameters are rc (reason code, indicating why a retarget happened, such as rc=1 to refer back to index 1) and mp (multiple point, indicating an alternate attempt that should not block further attempts, such as trying a PSTN number in parallel).

The index numbering scheme allows for a tree structure. The first address is index 1. If it is retargeted, the next address is 1.1. If that is retargeted again, it is 1.1.1. If the proxy also tries an alternate address in parallel, that is 1.2. This structure lets applications understand the decision tree that led to the current request.
sections.plainLanguage: Each History-Info entry is like a breadcrumb: a URI with an index number and a reason why it was tried. The index shows whether it is a retry, an alternate, or a chain of forwards.

sections.title: Practical Call Flow Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC documents 11 detailed use cases with full message flow diagrams. These include sequential forking (trying one address, then another on timeout), privacy considerations (hiding history from certain domains), automatic call distribution (distributing calls to available agents), determining which alias was used, voicemail integration (both corporate and consumer styles), GRUU (globally routable user agent URIs), and service invocation scenarios.

One example is sequential forking: Alice calls Bob. The proxy tries Bob's desk, gets no answer, and tries his office. If the office phone is also busy, the proxy tries his home. Each attempt is recorded in History-Info with an index that shows it is a sequential retry (1, 1.1, 1.2, and so on). When Alice receives the final response (486 Busy Here), the History-Info list shows her the path taken.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC shows 11 real scenarios: what happens when you call someone at multiple locations, how privacy works with forwarding, how voicemail sees the history, and other practical situations.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Implications
sections.content:
History-Info reveals the call path, which can expose sensitive information about a user's phone numbers and internal routing rules. The Privacy header field (RFC 3323) can suppress or anonymize History-Info across domain boundaries. An intermediary can add Privacy: history to prevent the history from being sent outside its domain. The RFC also describes how the optional rc parameter can be used to indicate the reason for a retarget (e.g., rc=1 for redirect, rc=302 for a 302 response code).

Operators who deploy History-Info should be aware that it expands the size of SIP messages and that applications must handle the additional complexity of parsing and interpreting the history. The RFC is informational, providing guidance on use cases rather than strict requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: History-Info can leak information about a user's secret phone numbers and routing. Privacy controls can hide the history from outside the company. Implementers should think about who gets to see the history.

sections.title: When and How to Use History-Info
sections.content:
Applications that benefit from History-Info include voicemail systems (which need to know which address rang before routing to voicemail), call centers (which need to understand why a call was distributed to an agent), and user devices (which can avoid calling the same number twice). The mp parameter is useful when the proxy is trying multiple addresses in parallel: it marks which entries are parallel attempts (should not affect the normal sequence) versus sequential fallbacks.

The RC (reason code) parameter can encode why a retarget happened: a 302 Moved Temporarily response, a timeout, or a policy decision. Applications can use this information to make smarter decisions about how to present the call path to the user or whether to attempt a number themselves. The RFC provides examples of consumer voicemail (which passes History-Info to the voicemail server so it knows the calling number) and corporate systems (which suppress history outside the company for privacy).
sections.plainLanguage: Voicemail, call centers, and apps need this information. The 'mp' tag marks alternate tries (do not count them as failures). The reason code says why the call was retargeted, so the app can make smart decisions.
